summary: What is EVA Marswalk? EVA Marswalk is an innovative, survival-centric navigation platform engineered to deliver terrain-aware surface pathfinding for astronauts traversing the Martian surface. By synthesizing multi-layered geospatial datasets from NASA missions—encompassing elevation, terrain slope, atmospheric pressure, gravity anomalies, dust, radiation, and surface temperature—the application bridges a critical gap in current planetary mapping tools, which remain restricted to macro-scale global views rather than human-scale surface excursions. As humanity prepares for crewed missions to Mars, explorers face life-or-death trade-offs between scientific discovery and survival, where rugged topography, intense radiation, and heavy equipment can rapidly deplete vital oxygen reserves. Powered by the Field D* pathfinding algorithm and a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) terrain cost grid, EVA Marswalk computes the safest and shortest traverse routes while modeling payload mass, optimal walking pace, and metabolic oxygen consumption against NASA xEMU spacesuit thresholds. Ultimately, our project empowers astronauts with immediate, data-driven safety assessments before stepping out of the habitat, ensuring every expedition across the Red Planet is safe, resource-efficient, and scientifically productive.

🌌 1. Overview & The Martian EVA Challenge

1.1 The Problem

Extravehicular activity (EVA) on Mars is constrained by unforgiving terrain and strict physiological limits. Deep fault scarps, volcanic shields rising over 21 km above the datum, impact crater rims, regional dust storms, and a thin carbon-dioxide atmosphere averaging ~610 Pa at the zero-elevation datum leave narrow operational safety margins. An astronaut traversing across high-grade regolith faces asymmetric downhill tipping hazards, sharp increases in metabolic oxygen consumption, and elevated solar/galactic cosmic radiation exposure.

1.2 Why Terrain-Aware EVA Planning Matters.

Shortest-path Euclidean routing fails in planetary exploration. A path that minimizes straight-line horizontal distance can force an astronaut up unstable slopes, through dusty depressions, or across uncompensated canyon drops that breach safety thresholds or exhaust oxygen supplies before safe return. Mission planners need continuous-angle terrain reasoning paired with transparent scientific data provenance so modeled estimates are never mistaken for raw spacecraft telemetry.

1.3 The Solution: EVA MARSWALK

EVA MARSWALK was built by Team AI-Powered—undergraduate students at the Ho Chi Minh University of Science (VNU-HCM), Vietnam—for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Running directly in the browser with zero external framework dependencies, it fuses bundled NASA PDS and USGS Astrogeology datasets (MGS MOLA GTM090AA, Viking MDIM 2.1, MRO120G / 120F, and MRO MCS 2025073120_DDR) with a background Web Worker pathfinding suite (Field D*, D* Lite, Fast Marching Method (FMM), and Baseline A*), dynamic Gaussian dust storm exclusion (tau >= 2.0, wind > 100 km/h, 48 h buffer), Mars-scaled Minetti metabolic modeling, and multi-scale 2D/3D WebGL inspection.

🏛️ 2. Strategic Architecture & NASA Open-Science Integration

2.1 Four Core Strategic Capabilities

1. Verifiable Planetary Data Fusion & Explicit Provenance: Every value displayed in the HUD or analytics modal explicitly distinguishes between Measured Orbital Datasets, Derived Physical Values, Modeled Estimates, and Visual Representations.
2. Bidirectional Slope-Coupled Locomotion & Metabolic Planning: Evaluates signed directional traversal slopes separately (+22.0° default uphill / -16.5° downhill for Astronaut EVA, plus configurable Robotic Rover 15.0° and Agile Scout 28.0° presets) alongside a Mars-scaled 5th-order Minetti metabolic energy model and physiological O₂ demand.
3. Spatiotemporal Dust Storm Hazard Exclusion & Detour Replanning: Models moving storm fronts across optical depth (τ), surface wind speed, and a 48 h spatiotemporal arrival buffer, isolating storm rejection cleanly from topographic failure (STORM_EXCLUSION vs. TOO_STEEP).
4. Multi-Paradigm Non-Blocking Worker Benchmarking: Offloads search execution across 4 distinct algorithmic engines onto geospatial/route_worker.js, benchmarking CPU latency, node expansions, distance, smoothness, and O₂ consumption side-by-side over identical terrain rasters.

2.2 Data-to-Decision Architecture

2.3 Multi-Scale Spatial Architecture

2.4 Integrated EVA Routing & Validation Workflow

2.5 Strict Severity Bottleneck & Survival Index (survivability.js)

For both site monitoring and route validation, evaluateAstronautSurvival() evaluates environmental parameters against proximity coefficient curves p and assigns SAFE, CAUTION, UNSAFE, or UNKNOWN:

  • Strict Categorical Dominance: UNSAFE > CAUTION > UNKNOWN > SAFE. If even one criterion fails an UNSAFE bound, the entire location or corridor is flagged UNSAFE (S_overall = 0.5 * S_total), preventing safe averages on benign metrics from hiding a lethal threat. Two or more CAUTION flags also halve S_overall, whereas a single CAUTION applies a 0.8 multiplier.
    • Jezero Crater (18.38°N, 77.58°E): Flat crater floor (~0.6° slope, -2,500 m elevation, ~771–773 Pa modeled pressure) typically evaluates SAFE (99/100) with an 8.0 h nominal EVA window.
    • Olympus Mons Summit (18.65°N, 226.2°E): Despite gentle summit shield slopes, extreme altitude (~21.2 km) drives modeled barometric pressure down to ~84–99 Pa (far below the 180 Pa critical limit), triggering an immediate decompression UNSAFE (38/100) warning.

2.6 Data Provenance Taxonomy

2.7 Pathfinding Suite & Scenario-Dependent Benchmarking

All four solvers implemented in geospatial/field_d_star.js (_runFieldDStar, _runDStarLite, _runFMM, _runAStar) run against the same MOLA elevation/slope grids and the shared evaluateTerrainTransition() cost evaluator:

Note!

Scenario-Dependent Benchmark Outcomes: Efficiency gains (such as distance or O₂ saved vs. Baseline A*) are computed dynamically per route inside runFourAlgorithmBenchmark() (o2SavedVsAStarPct). Measured savings vary by route geometry, local slope roughness, optimization objective (min_risk, min_energy, min_elevation, balanced), and obstacle density—there is no fixed universal percentage across all Martian terrains.

Battery Telemetry & Consumables Clarification

Per geospatial/eva_analytics.js, the PLSS Battery (20.5 V × 40 Ah / 820 Wh LIB) and 8.0 h Max EVA Limit are displayed strictly as REFERENCE SPEC / NOT MODELED. The engine computes mechanical/metabolic work equivalent (Wh) alongside dynamic oxygen (L) depletion, and does not simulate active electrical battery drain from suit avionics, ventilation fans, heaters, or cooling pumps.

✨ 3. Key Features

3.1 Custom Multi-Layer 2D Mars Explorer

(geospatial/equirectangular_map.js): Four-canvas pipeline rendering a verified 72-tile Viking MDIM 2.1 and MOLA 4-tier LOD pyramid plus 8 selectable scientific layers (main, elevation, pressure, gravity_120g, slope, surface_g, geoid_n, gravity_delta) with an off-thread createImageBitmap LRU cache.

3.2 Custom WebGL 3D Mars Globe

(mars_3d_map.html): Interactive 3D planetary sphere built directly on native WebGL shaders without external globe or mapping libraries, supporting 1x–10x radial terrain displacement, 6 switchable global scalar textures plus packed elevation/geoid textures, 13 pinned planetary landmarks, and 1,153 MRO MCS sounding track overlays.

3.3 Interactive Local 3D Terrain Block

(geospatial/terrain_view_3d.js): Drag the 3D TERRAIN Pegman astronaut onto any spot on Mars to inspect a 40° × 40° (~2,366 km wide) 97 × 97 vertex (18,432 triangles) MOLA heightfield with Visual, MOLA, and Slope shading.

3.4 Marswalk Planner & Background Worker

(geospatial/route_worker.js): Non-blocking route calculation with corridor safety buffers (0.40·C, 0.75·C, 1.00·C), directional uphill/downhill limits, customizable biomechanics (speed, bodyMass, equipmentMass, oxygenCapacity), and 4 optimization objectives.

3.5 Dynamic Dust Storm Simulator

(geospatial/dust_storm_simulator.js): Spawns moving 2D Gaussian storm cells (R = 20–600 km, Weak to Severe, compass vector 0°–359°, velocity 0–100 km/h) with hard τ >= 2.0, wind > 100 km/h, and 48 h arrival separation constraints.

3.6 Animated Astronaut Walk & Analytics HUD

(geospatial/eva_analytics.js): 1×–200× mission playback paired with 6 synchronized KPI cards, coupled Speed/VO₂ & DEM elevation SVG plots, and raw LaTeX export of active equations.

3.7 Gazetteer Search, 7 Themes & Bilingual UI

(geospatial/eva_settings.js): Fly directly to coordinates or features across 18 2D quick presets, 13 3D globe pins, 19 MARS_LANDMARKS, and 27 searchable IAU/USGS entries in geospatial/mars_gazetteer.js, wrapped in 7 synchronized CSS themes and an ENG / VIE language toggle.

📖 4. How Does EVA MARSWALK Work?

A Complete Step-by-Step User Tutorial

4.1. Getting Started & Launching the Workspace (For Local Use, Skipped if you use Live Demo)

1.Run desktop/launch_desktop.bat on Windows (or python desktop/server.py index.html from the repository root) and visit http://localhost:8080/index.html (or use the hosted web demo).
2. Always serve over HTTP rather than opening .html via file://, so the browser can load tile manifests, binary grids, and route_worker.js.
3. Use the top-right ENG | VIE toggle on any page to switch languages, and choose Open 2D map → (mars_2d_map.html) or Open 3D explorer → (mars_3d_map.html).
Figure 1: The EVA MARSWALK Mission Portal (index.html) showing the ENG | VIE toggle and entry cards for the 2D Explorer and 3D Globe Explorer

4.2. Exploring Mars with the 2D Explorer

1. Click and drag on mars_2d_map.html to pan across 0°–360°E, 90°S–90°N, or click directly inside GLOBAL LOCATOR (0°–360°E) (bottom-left).
2. Scroll with the mouse wheel or use + / - and Home (Reset View) on the bottom-right stack to inspect sharper LOD pyramid tiers (1.00x up to 250.0x).
3. Click any point on Mars to place the red target crosshair, read the bottom-left LAT / LON readout, and toggle surface labels using the Map Pin button.


Figure 2: The 2D Explorer main canvas with the top command bar, collapsed Layer Ribbon (▲), right-edge tool launchers, GLOBAL LOCATOR, bottom Settings button, and 3D TERRAIN Pegman.

4.3. Navigating with Fly To, Coordinates & Gazetteer

EVA MARSWALK uses Latitude (-90° to +90°) and Planetocentric East Longitude (0° to 360°E) in lat, lon order (e.g., 18.38, 77.58 for Jezero Crater).

Figure 3: Zooming into Jezero Crater (18.38°N, 77.58°E) via Fly To—showing the zoomed basemap, crosshair callout, and updated GLOBAL LOCATOR footprint.

4.4. Switching Scientific Data Layers (2D Ribbon)

Click the centered ▲ tab below the top bar to expand the Scientific Data Layer Ribbon, select any of the 8 layers, and read the bottom Scale: bar alongside the live Selected: cursor value. Remember that visual brightness in Main RGB is surface albedo, not elevation—switch to MOLA Elevation or Terrain Slope to judge physical steepness.

Figure 4: Expanded top layer ribbon with MOLA Elevation active (-8,201 m to +21,241 m) showing deep dark basins and bright volcanic highlands.

4.5. Exploring the 3D Mars Globe

1. Switch to 3D Globe Explorer (mars_3d_map.html) from the portal or top bar.
2. Adjust 3D TERRAIN RELIEF (1x, 2x, 5x, 10x) and SPACE DISPLAY (Lat/Lon Grid 30°, Pin 13 Landmarks, Auto-Rotate, Layer Opacity), or toggle MCS Sounding Tracks (1,153).
3. Click any point on the sphere to inspect ASTRONAUT SURVIVAL MONITOR and expand DETAILS ▼ on SELECTED LOCATION for Cartesian (X, Y, Z) coordinates, planetary radius, gravity anomaly, and MCS atmospheric profiles when covered by a track.Figure 5: 3D Globe Explorer centered on Olympus Mons (5.0x relief) with ASTRONAUT SURVIVAL MONITOR flagging DANGEROUS (38/100) due to low summit pressure.

Figure 6: Expanded DETAILS ▼ geophysical card on the 3D Globe displaying Cartesian (X, Y, Z), planetary radius, MOLA height, and gravity anomaly.

4.6. Monitoring Astronaut Safety

Click the Astronaut Monitoring button on the right-edge tool rail in 2D Explorer (or inspect the right panel on 3D Globe) and expand Mission Details ▲ / ▼ to view temperature, barometric pressure, terrain slope, airborne dust (τ), radiation estimate, Estimated Safe EVA Window, and local warnings.Figure 7: ASTRONAUT MONITORING at Jezero Crater showing SAFE (99/100) and expanded 6-layer planetary telemetry.

4.7. Planning a Marswalk Mission

1. Open Marswalk Planner (top icon on the right rail).
2. Set Starting Point (S) and Destination (D) via Gazetteer search, decimal coordinates, or Select Start/Destination on Map. (Use ⇅ Swap Start / Destination to test the reverse direction for uphill/downhill asymmetry.)
3. Adjust Walking Speed (0.1–15.0 m/s, default 1.2 m/s), Body Mass (default 80 kg), Equip Mass (default 15 kg, +50 kg NASA xEMU added automatically = 145.0 kg), and O₂ Cap (default 480.0 L in UI).
4. Pick an Optimization Objective (Minimum Risk, Minimum Energy Consumption, Minimum Elevation Variation, or Balanced Optimization), tune weights if desired, and click 🚀 Calculate Route.Figure 8: Configuring Start (18.41°N, 77.69°E) and Destination (17.60°N, 79.10°E) inside Marswalk Planner before execution.

Figure 9: Generated continuous Field D* path with Route Telemetry Summary and an expected O₂ DEFICIT WARNING on a regional 187.9 km traverse under a 480 L single-EVA tank.

4.8. Comparing Pathfinding Algorithms

Click Algorithms in the header (or Configure ⚡ inside Marswalk Planner) to switch active solvers or click 🔄 Re-Run Benchmark on Current Map to compare Field D*, D* Lite, Fast Marching (FMM), and Baseline A* on CPU time, expanded nodes, distance, O₂ burn, and smoothness.

Figure 10: Algorithms & Benchmark Suite comparing all four algorithms side-by-side on identical Jezero Crater terrain.

4.9. Running the Simulated Astronaut Walk

After generating a route, scroll down in Marswalk Planner to Simulated Astronaut Walk, select a playback multiplier (1× up to 200×), and click ▶ Start Walk to animate traversal with real-time position, speed, segment slope (θ), and local storm telemetry updates.Figure 11: Mid-traversal playback at 200× Sim updating coordinate progress, Sim Time, Sim Dist, and segment slope (θ).

4.10. Simulating and Avoiding Dust Storms

Open the 🌪️ Dust Storm tab (middle rail icon).
Click + Add Storm (or 📍 Place Storm on Mars Map), set Radius (R) (20–600 km), intensity (Weak / Moderate / Strong / Severe), propagation direction (0°–359°), and movement velocity (0–100 km/h).
Advance time with ▶ Simulate Storm Movement, +1h, or +6h, then re-run 🚀 Calculate Route. Storms breaching tau >= 2.0, wind > 100 km/h, or the 48h arrival buffer force autonomous detours or cleanly abort with STORM_EXCLUSION.Figure 12: Active DUST STORM #1 (Strong, R = 320 km, Peak Wind: 75 km/h) rendered with its dashed hazard perimeter and propagation arrow.

4.11. Inspecting Biophysical Analytics

Click Analytics in the top header after computing a route (use 🔄 Sync Telemetry after changing suit parameters) to inspect the 6 KPI cards, coupled Walking Speed & Oxygen Flow SVG plot, DEM Elevation Profile, Coupled Martian EVA Mathematical Model, and raw LaTeX export.Figure 13: Analytics Dashboard synchronized to an active Jezero Crater traverse with speed, VO₂, elevation profile, and live parameter formulas.

4.12. Inspecting Local 3D Terrain on the Spot

Drag the 3D TERRAIN astronaut Pegman (bottom-right of 2D Explorer) onto any location and release it to open the MARS TERRAIN VIEW WebGL modal (40° × 40°, ~2,366 km regional patch). Orbit with left-drag, pan with right-drag, adjust Exag: - 5x +, and switch between Visual, MOLA, and Slope modes.

Figure 14: MARS TERRAIN VIEW WebGL patch centered on Jezero Crater (18.41°N, 77.69°E) with 5x vertical exaggeration.

4.13. Customizing Themes, Constraints & Settings

Click Settings in the bottom-left footer of the 2D Explorer (changes persist via localStorage across all pages):

8 Settings Tabs: Appearance (7 UI themes—Cartographic Paper, Rosé Pine Moon / Dusk default, Studio Graphite & Muted Sage, USGS Cartographic Light, Martian Regolith, NASA JPL Tactical, Classic AI Slate), Maps & Offline Data, Navigation & Sensors, Profile & Constraints, Power & Performance (60 FPS vs. 30 FPS + Purge Local Bitmap Cache), Safety & Survival, UI / HUD Display, and Future Developments (all unimplemented roadmap items, detailed under 🚀 Future Developments).Figure 15: Settings → Appearance displaying all 7 synchronized interface themes.Figure 16: Settings → Profile & Constraints configuring Astronaut EVA (22.0°), Robotic Rover (15.0°), or Agile Scout (28.0°) directional slopes and the 3-ring Route Safety Clearance corridor.

🚀 6. Quick Start & Installation

EVA MARSWALK runs directly from static web files with zero compilation steps, build toolchains, or external databases.
Try Online Immediately: https://sm9038.github.io/Extravehicular-Activity-EVA-/

Prerequisites
+Modern browser supporting HTML5 Canvas, WebGL, and ES6 Module Web Workers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari).
+Python 3.8+ (for running the local HTTP file server so fetch(), manifests, and module Web Workers work without file:// CORS blocks).

Option 1: Windows One-Click Launchers
1. Double-click desktop\launch_2d_map.bat to open 2D Mars Explorer & Marswalk Planner (mars_2d_map.html), or
2. Double-click desktop\launch_desktop.bat to open the Mission Control Portal (index.html).

Option 2: Cross-Platform Terminal (Recommended Locally)Option 3: Python Built-In HTTP Server Fallback
Then open http://localhost:8080/index.html, http://localhost:8080/mars_2d_map.html, or http://localhost:8080/mars_3d_map.html.

Warning !
Always use http://localhost:... rather than file:///.... Browsers block module Web Workers (geospatial/route_worker.js) and fetch() calls to local JSON manifests over file:// URLs.

🛠️ 8. Tech Stack & Verified System Architecture

+Frontend: Vanilla ES6+ JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3 custom variable theming system (7 synchronized themes across index.html, mars_2d_map.html, mars_3d_map.html).
+2D & 3D Graphics: Custom 4-canvas 2D tiler (equirectangular_map.js) + custom raw WebGL shaders (mars_3d_map.html sphere & terrain_view_3d.js regional block), built directly on native browser Canvas and WebGL APIs.
+Concurrency: Module Web Worker (geospatial/route_worker.js) preventing UI blocking during multi-hundred-thousand-node terrain searches.
+Local Server: Python 3 http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer (desktop/server.py) + Windows .bat wrappers; no backend database required.

⚠️ 9. Scientific Limitations & Disclaimers.

9.1. Academic & Simulation Scope Only:

EVA MARSWALK is an undergraduate competition prototype, not operational aerospace or flight-planning software.

9.2. Global Grid Resolution vs. Meter-Scale Hazards:

Global 720 × 360 routing grids (0.5°/px, ~30 km equator cell spacing) and planetary DEM tiles resolve macro-topography (volcanic shields, chasm walls, large crater rims), not meter-scale boulders, soft regolith drifts, or sharp overhang hazards that require HiRISE/rover verification.

9.3. Modeled Environmental Approximations:

Ambient pressure outside MCS tracks uses an isothermal hydrostatic scale height (210 K, omitting seasonal CO₂ frost condensation cycles and tropospheric lapse rates); ambient temperature and GCR attenuation use latitude/pressure proxies; dust storms are synthetic Gaussian hazard fields (MODELED).

9.4. Static Battery Specification (Not Modeled):

PLSS battery labels (20.5 V × 40 Ah / 820 Wh) and 8.0 h limits are static reference specifications; avionics/fan/heater electrical discharge is not simulated.

9.5. Single-Leg Point-to-Point Optimization:

Marswalk Planner optimizes one leg (Start → Destination) per run rather than coupled outbound-plus-return closed loops; use ⇅ Swap Start / Destination to evaluate return-leg asymmetry.
